body.text: Anthropic's record-breaking IPO fails to calm AI jitters as tech stocks fall further
In short:
Technology shares have fallen across the world after Anthropic's market debut.
Following its initial public offering, shares rocketed to more than $US110 ($166) before falling below $US90.
Nvidia also shed value, while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 fell in value by the end of the week.

Technology shares have nosedived and dragged stocks into the red across the world, after AI firm Anthropic's bumper market debut failed to dispel growing worries about the sector's massive investments and sky-high valuations.

Anthropic shares briefly rocketed from an initial offering price of $US83 ($125) to more than $US110 on Thursday, despite a broader sell-off on Wall Street, but fell back sharply with the price plunging back below $US90 after Friday morning trades.

"The performance of the shares over the coming days and weeks could provide one of the clearest tests yet of whether investors believe the enormous sums being poured into AI will ultimately generate attractive returns," said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.
While Anthropic surged on its Nasdaq debut, the tech-dominated index struggled for the rest of the day and was 3.2 per cent further down after Friday morning trading.
New York's broader S&P 500, which also trades the shares of the world's biggest tech companies, shed 2 per cent on Thursday and continued to fall on Friday, extending a major run of losses.
The benchmark S&P 500 index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10 per cent from its October 6 all-time high.
The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market.

Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction.
They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the market's big slide.

"We think the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 have further to run," wrote James Reilly, from Capital Economics, who said the prospect of an "AI bust in 2027" was his central forecast and a growing worry for investors.
"This doesn't mean we think the technology is a dud, nor that demand will collapse. But the revenue hurdle to justify the scale of AI investment looks very demanding,"
Mr Reilly said.
AI stocks have been losing ground partly due to worries their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified.

Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data centre construction winning at federal and state levels.

"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird.
Dr Sue Keay of the University of NSW AI Institute told ABC News it was a bit early to suggest the AI bubble had burst.
"I think it is showing that investors are actually starting to examine the long-term viability of these companies and whether they really can be valued at over $1 trillion," Dr Keay said.
"One of the challenges with the Anthropic IPO has been that in raising $81bn, that's essentially taking $81bn out of the capital markets that could have been invested elsewhere.

"I think on the one hand, it shows that people still do have confidence in AI as a business, but the fact that most of the investment is only happening in a handful of companies means that the benefits really aren't being distributed and so we do have quite a high concentration risk because we're not funding a range of different AI businesses."

Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department's move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further restrictions on the sector.

Chip stocks including Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI build-out tanked as well, including optical products company Corning and energy provider Bloom Energy.
The falls followed Nvidia's high-profile founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, resigning following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.
The chip giant, which has endured a long period of losses, slumped by 6.9 per cent by midday in New York on Friday, despite posting massive profits earlier in the week.
In Asian trading on Friday, the Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei stock markets — home to the region's leading AI-linked firms — tumbled between 5 and 6.2 per cent.

Europe's main stock markets all fell back significantly by close of trading, with shares in French video game maker Ubisoft slumping more than 20 per cent after it posted a bigger first-half loss than expected.
The report came amid the worldwide hype surrounding Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest in the hugely popular Rockstar Games series that is shaping up to be the biggest entertainment launch ever.
While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.

The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared with last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections.
Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the US war with Iran.
AFP/AP
